opus-5.5.text:
I think it varies a lot, and it depends mostly on how close you are to the frontier work.

Inside the labs, among the people actually training models, the feeling is quite intense. You see capabilities move week by week, and things that seemed far away a year ago are now routine. People there talk about timelines very concretely, and many genuinely believe we're in a period that will look historic later. That excitement also comes with some anxiety: about competition, about safety, and about whether we understand what we're building.

One step out, in the broader tech industry, startups, VCs, and big companies adopting AI, the excitement is real but feels different. It's more about products, markets, and who captures the value. There's enthusiasm, but also fatigue and skepticism, because there's so much hype and many demos don't become reliable products. Some people feel the gap between what models can do on a benchmark and what they can do inside a messy real workflow.

Then there are people in Silicon Valley who aren't in AI directly, and for them it's sometimes just background noise, or even a source of worry about jobs and whether their own work will matter.

So there's a gradient. The closer you are to the model, the more you feel it's not hype but something underestimated. The farther away, the more it looks like another tech cycle. Personally, I think the truth is that the underlying progress is real and fast, but turning it into broad real-world impact takes longer than insiders expect. Both views capture part of the picture.

r001.rationale: It contrasts intense excitement among people training models with product- and market-focused excitement in the broader tech industry, making the difference depend on proximity to model work versus products.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the excitement is actually quite uneven, and the unevenness is interesting.

If you're inside the big labs, the people who are closest to the frontier are, honestly, the most excited, and I don't think that's just because they're paid to be. When you watch the models improve month to month, and especially when you see a capability show up that you didn't explicitly train for, it's hard not to feel like something real is happening. That feeling compounds. People in the labs have a sort of internal timeline that's shorter than what the outside sees.

Then there's a second ring, which is the broader startup and VC world. There the excitement is more like a market signal. It's loud, there's a lot of money, but it's also more fragile, because it tracks demos and valuations rather than the underlying curve. Some of those people were equally excited about things that didn't pan out, so you have to discount a bit.

And then there's a third group that I actually find most interesting, which is researchers who've been in the field for a long time, often from the more academic side. A lot of them are more skeptical, and not in a dismissive way. They've seen hype cycles before. They'll point out that benchmarks saturate, that scaling has costs, that we don't really understand why things work. I think that skepticism is healthy and the field needs it, even if I personally lean toward the optimistic side.

One thing I'd add: the gap between these groups has been widening, not narrowing. The people who are most excited are becoming more so, and the people who are skeptical are becoming more entrenched. That's partly because the evidence is genuinely ambiguous. If you look at agents, for instance, the capability jumps are real, but so is the gap between a nice demo and something that reliably works in the world. Depending on which half of that you weigh, you end up with very different feelings. So in some sense the variation in excitement reflects a real disagreement about what counts as progress, not just differences in temperament.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts frontier lab researchers with startup and VC circles, but it does not clearly frame excitement as depending on whether someone works on products or models.

astra-6.text:
I think Silicon Valley is far from uniform. People working directly on models might be excited about a particular research result, while people building applications are asking whether that progress actually makes their product more useful. And investors may be excited about a different question: how big the market could become.

Even among researchers, you can be very optimistic about the long-term potential and still feel that today’s systems have substantial limitations. Those views aren’t contradictory. Sometimes being close to the technology makes you more excited because you see what’s possible, and sometimes it makes you more cautious because you see how often it fails.

So I would distinguish excitement about capabilities, excitement about products, and excitement about business opportunities. They reinforce one another, but they don’t necessarily move at the same speed.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts model researchers’ excitement about research results with application builders’ focus on whether progress improves their products.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Silicon Valley can look uniformly excited about AI from the outside, but there’s actually a pretty wide range. Even among people who are very optimistic, the source of that excitement is different. Researchers might be excited about a new capability, founders about a product that has suddenly become possible, and investors about how large the market could become.

There’s also a difference between believing the technology will be transformative and believing it’s ready for a particular application today. You can be very optimistic about the next ten years and still be frustrated by how unreliable a model is on your own task. So someone can sound skeptical in a product discussion and extremely bullish in a conversation about the future. Those positions are quite compatible.

r001.rationale: It links different sources of excitement to different roles: researchers focus on new capabilities, while founders focus on newly possible products. This conveys a research/model-work versus product-work distinction.
